Toby David (Chief of Staff) attended solo to add transparency on the Pepsi inventory situation first disclosed the prior week at Barclays.

Core message: PepsiCo (Celsius's largest customer, ~55%+ of NA purchases) purchased ~$100-120M less in Q3 2024 vs Q3 2023 because Pepsi over-stocked Celsius product in 2023 (its first full year as distributor) and is now drawing inventory down to a normalized, optimized level ('cash is king').
Management stressed this is an order/timing issue, not a demand issue: scanner growth ~10% QTD YoY with market share up ~1 point, and depletions out of Pepsi warehouses match scanner data.
Pepsi's dynamic ordering system is relatively new and gives little Q4 visibility; management hopes the 'bigger swings are behind us' but would not commit.
Sugar-free is now 50% of the category; Celsius is #2 with ~25% sugar-free share; YTD full-sugar energy down ~4% while sugar-free up ~7% - trends favor Celsius.

Category slowdown is a frequency/intensification issue plus slower new-consumer entry, which hurts Celsius disproportionately given its over-index on new-to-category consumers; consumers are NOT leaving energy for coffee/tea/soda.
Celsius's broad, fruit-forward flavor assortment contrasts with Red Bull/Monster 'super SKUs' (operationally efficient power SKUs); today's consumer wants something different.

Celsius's value to retailers comes from bringing new-to-category consumers (not brand shifting) plus a strong basket ring, keeping 2025 retailer meetings 'excellent' even with velocity challenged; management declined space guidance.

Amazon (where Celsius is #1 over 18 months at ~20+ share, and is not space-constrained) is cited as a barometer of share capability; tracked-channel share has been roughly flat at ~11-12% for 3.5-4 months amid a stagnant category.

International is only ~5% of sales vs ~40% for Monster; Canada launched Jan 2024 and jumped to a ~5 share (#4 brand) within months with Pepsi as the distributor; UK/Ireland launched with Suntory (positive Tesco reads); Australia/New Zealand entries within a couple of months.
International market-entry approach is market-dependent: fitness as the early investment then a core partner retailer (e.g., Tesco); going too wide too fast risks delisting.

Competitors are aggressive on promotions (Monster running BOGOs on Reign, Bang and core brands); Celsius does not promote deeper than peers ('probably below most') but is getting 'promotionally more motivated' in Q3 with shallow-depth tactics given the tight consumer.

Margin: Q3 will have 'a lot of noise' from the ~$120M Pepsi order shortfall undercutting budgeted margin structure, with a little Q4 noise before returning to the margin framework; Monster is a 'great comp' but its gross margin excludes outbound freight (~4% difference).

U.S. growth comes from three levers: TDP expansion, velocity and innovation; Essentials launched in 2024 targeting an incremental consumer; management seeks 'white space' within the Pepsi portfolio so Pepsi leans into innovation.

Pepsi relationship has some partnership-driven category preclusions but management does not view it as blocking anything Celsius would pursue; food service is ~12% of Pepsi sales (vending the big portion), in 'early innings' with plenty of growth runway.
How has the inventory situation evolved, and what should investors know for thinking about Q3?

David: at the prior week's Barclays conference Celsius pre-announced that Pepsi (~55%+ of NA purchases) purchased ~$100-120M less in Q3 vs Q3 PY; Pepsi over-stocked in 2023 (first full year as distributor) and is now optimizing inventory. Celsius scanner growth is ~10% QTD with share up ~1 point - orders should line up but do not because Pepsi is drawing down inventory; Celsius is 'very comfortable' with Pepsi's current inventory level for servicing the account, but it impacts Q3 reported numbers.
Does this 'rip the band-aid off' and set inventory at the right level, or could further adjustments come?

David declined to discuss Q4, citing lack of visibility - Pepsi's dynamic ordering system is relatively new. He would 'like to think' an adjustment of this magnitude gets Pepsi much closer to a normalized inventory level and that 'the bigger swings are behind us,' but would not commit.
How does the slowing category break down between sugared and sugar-free energy, and how is Celsius positioned?

David: sugar-free is now 50% of the category and where the trends are; Celsius is the strong #2 with ~25% sugar-free share. YTD full-sugar energy down ~4% while sugar-free up ~7%. The category is not losing consumers to other categories - it is a frequency/intensification issue with slower new-consumer entry that affects Celsius more given its new-to-category over-index; confident Celsius will be well positioned once the category normalizes in 2025.
Shelf resets, assortment breadth & distribution trajectory
How should shelf resets be modeled, where does distribution go from here given slower category growth, and is a broad assortment helpful vs the Red Bull/Monster super-SKU model?

David: Red Bull/Monster have operationally efficient super SKUs but today's consumer wants something different (Celsius's fruit-forward flavors); spring resets occurred a few months ago, with cut-ins/retailer-exclusive SKUs through the year and most current meetings for 2025 ('very positive'); declined space guidance. Celsius's retailer value is new-to-category consumers plus a strong basket ring; energy is the 'jewel of beverage' and would at minimum retain its space and possibly gain space from weaker, lower-margin categories.
Celsius is ~11-12% share - how should investors think about the headroom and benchmark the opportunity?

David: management is careful not to issue share guidance, but Amazon (where Celsius is #1 over 18 months at ~20+ share, not space-constrained) is a good barometer of capability; strong US markets - South Florida (mid-20s, #2), NYC (~20%), several in the upper teens. Share has been roughly flat for 3.5-4 months amid a stagnant category, but management is confident about the 2025 opportunity once the category normalizes.
Update on international progress and approach across Canada, UK/Ireland, and the upcoming France/Australia/New Zealand launches?

David: Canada launched Jan 2024 and jumped to ~5 share (#4 brand) within months, with Pepsi as distributor; the UK is one of the largest energy markets and an important proof point since international (~5% of sales vs ~40% for Monster) is largely not in the valuation; methodical approach, not overinvesting, 'more fuel on the fire' if markets succeed; UK/Ireland launched with Suntory into many Tesco stores with 'very positive' reads; Australia/New Zealand entries within a couple of months, more announcements soon.
Is gym/fitness branding the initial approach, and is market entry phased to build brand identity with a core consumer first?

David: it depends by market - Canada went nationwide quickly given US proximity and marketing bleed-over, whereas other markets start with fitness as the early investment then a core partner retailer (e.g., Tesco). Going too wide too fast requires creating pull-through everywhere or risks delisting; concentrating on one big retailer focuses marketing resources, secures retailer lean-in via exclusivity, and builds a selling story for broader distribution.
How does the US promotional environment look, is there extra intensity, and is slowness driving pricing changes or irrational promotions?

David: peers are aggressive; pushed back on Nielsen data calling Celsius 'over promotional' - Celsius uses Circana, and Nielsen counts off-shelf displays (where Celsius over-indexes) as promotions; Celsius does not promote deeper than peers, 'probably below most.' BOGOs are prevalent (Monster on Reign, Bang and core brands); Celsius is getting 'promotionally more motivated' in Q3 with shallow-depth tactics (e.g., two for $4.50 vs two for $4) mainly to secure off-shelf displays in a category ~26 weeks/year on promotion.
Celsius already has strong margins - what is the upside from here, and is Monster the right benchmark?

David: Q3 will have 'a lot of noise' because the ~$120M Pepsi order shortfall undercuts the budgeted margin structure, with a little Q4 noise before returning to the margin framework (Q2 2024 was ~52% gross profit). Monster historically excluded outbound freight from gross margin (a ~4% difference - so a Monster 59% equates to ~55% for Celsius); Celsius S&M is 21-23% of revenue, above Monster's, expected to come down with leverage; Celsius can avoid Monster's large US-vs-international margin delta since it is not contractually locked into one international distribution partner.
What role does innovation play, what might be ahead (citing Essentials), and how far might the brand extend into adjacencies?

David: U.S. growth comes from three areas - TDP expansion, velocity and innovation. Essentials launched in 2024 has 'done well,' targeting an incremental consumer that will take time to reach core-brand velocity; management is evaluating other areas within energy and adjacent categories, identifying 'white space opportunities within the Pepsi portfolio' so Pepsi leans into innovation.
Does the Pepsi relationship have explicit limitations on what kind of products Celsius can launch?

David: unsure what has been publicly disclosed; Pepsi has some partnerships that would preclude certain areas, but he did not think it was blocking Celsius from anything it would be looking to get into.
What does the food service opportunity look like (restaurants, universities, vending), and how much has been tackled vs what lies ahead?

David: food service is ~12% of Pepsi sales on a quarterly basis (vending a big portion, plus colleges, universities, hospitals, hotels, restaurants); Celsius feels it is in the 'early innings,' declined a target mix (the goal is to grow the total Pepsi business), and sees 'plenty of room' for growth; Celsius pairs better with meals than competitors with a more traditional energy taste.
